## Read-only subcommands broken out

The table is now keyed by command *path*, so the eight safe subcommands inside the two task-driven groups surface directly in the allow list:

content.text:
Four real findings. Ranked.

## 1. [High] The breakout skipped the one family that actually gets used

The census that justifies this PR: `trail` **185 invocations**, `checkpoint` 6, `session` 1. I broke out read-only subcommands for the two least-used families and left the most-used one flat:

```
trail show        Show a trail            ← read-only
trail list        List recent trails      ← read-only
trail approvals   List approval decisions ← read-only
trail watch       Tail a trail's events   ← read-only
```

All four now sit behind a `trail → task-driven` label reading *"writes data or spends tokens."* Before this PR the listing was flat and said nothing; now it actively discourages the read-only commands in the highest-traffic family. That's a plausible behavior regression, and it inverts the PR's own stated goal.

Fix: add `trail` to `agentHelpBreakoutGroups` and classify its 13 children (4 read-only, 9 task-driven).

## 2. [Medium] The text drill-down silently drops what `--json` carries

```
$ entire agent-help checkpoint
Subcommands: explain · list · policy · search · tokens     ← no audience

$ entire agent-help checkpoint --json
explain read-only … policy task-driven                     ← audience present
```

An agent drilling in via text — the default path — cannot tell `policy` from `list`. This breaks the repo's own agent-safe-fallback rule ("plain text output is acceptable when it contains the full information needed"), which my own test comment cites while the code violates it. Self-inflicted in this PR.

## 3. [Medium] Half the documented rule has no CI guard

The rule is "a group is read-only only if every advertised subcommand is." `TestAgentHelpAudiences_CoverEveryAdvertisedCommand` enforces classification for top-level commands and breakout-group children — but not for **read-only groups**. Live instance:

```
tokens          → classified read-only
tokens profile  → unclassified, no audience in --json
```

Benign today (`profile` really is read-only), but a future `tokens purge` would inherit the "changes nothing" heading with nothing failing. That is precisely the failure mode the guard exists to prevent, on the branch of the rule I didn't cover.

## 4. [Low] The evidence is stated more broadly than it is

`CLAUDE.md` now permanently records "A census of 963 agent transcripts found zero invocations…" without noting it is **one machine, one developer (you)**. The PR body says "a heavy-use machine"; the repo docs don't. Related: zero invocations proves agents never *ran* the commands, not that the recommendation had no effect — I can't distinguish "never read" from "read and correctly judged inapplicable." Neither weakens the decision (the token cost and the always-do framing are real regardless), but the docs assert it as settled general fact.

## One thing I checked that is *not* a bug

`checkpoint policy` is experimental and hidden in stable builds, which would make every *advertised* child of `checkpoint` read-only there — seemingly contradicting the task-driven label. It isn't: per `CLAUDE.md`, experimental gating controls visibility only and the command stays runnable. Task-driven is correct in both builds.

---

Findings 1–3 are all in code I wrote in this PR, and 1 is worth fixing before merge. Want me to push fixes for 1–3 (and soften the CLAUDE.md wording for 4), or leave the PR as-is and file them?

I feel the issue is that the bigger the help gets the less it make sense, I wonder if we rather should only show the commands that make sense to use, and then hide it behind deeper commands, but not sure

You're right, and it's worse than it looks: my own finding #1 would have made it worse. Adding `trail`'s breakout means +4 more lines, and every future group with mixed subcommands adds more. The listing is now 45 lines. I optimized "is this answer complete?" when the real constraint is "will an agent read this and act?"

The deeper mistake: I encoded a 2-D matrix (command × safety) as a flat list, so completeness costs a line per cell. Two fixes fall out of that, and they compose.

**Collapse the safety split back onto the group line** — one line instead of five, and it kills finding #2 as a side effect:

```
  checkpoint   Inspect checkpoints — explain/list/search/tokens read-only; policy writes
```

**Stop listing what the agent must not run.** 15 of 33 entries are user-owned. Spending 15 lines to say "don't" is backwards — one sentence says it better.

Here's the whole thing at that shape:

```
When to use entire — what's useful mid-task:

  status       Where Entire stands in this repo                       read-only
  trail        Branch trails — show/list/approvals/watch read-only;
               create/update/delete/approve/comment/… write
  checkpoint   Inspect checkpoints — explain/list/search/tokens
               read-only; policy writes
  session      Agent sessions — current/info/list/tokens read-only;
               adopt/attach/resume/stop write
  why          Why a line exists                                      read-only
  search       Search checkpoints, commits, sessions                  read-only
  api          Authenticated request to Entire's HTTP API             writes

Setup (enable, configure, auth), admin (org, project, repo, grant), and paid
multi-agent runs (review, investigate) are the user's to start — suggest them,
don't run them. `entire agent-help <command>` works for every command, listed
or not; `entire help` shows the full surface.
```

~12 lines against 45, and it answers *both* agent questions — is entire relevant here, and may I run it — without a taxonomy.

**On "hide behind deeper commands": yes, and the safety property is that nothing becomes unreachable.** `agent-help <cmd>` already resolves anything advertised, so curating the default view costs discoverability only for commands an agent shouldn't be initiating anyway. That satisfies the repo's agent-safe-fallback rule — the information is one explicit, signposted command away.

**The real risk is curation drift**: someone adds a genuinely agent-relevant command and it never appears. Mitigation is structural — make "listed" a field in the same CI-guarded table rather than a second list, so adding a command still forces the decision. The two questions are genuinely orthogonal (*shown?* and *safe?*), so that's a small struct rather than a wider enum — which is arguably the bug in my current design: I fused them into one axis and the listing inherited the fusion.

This does discard the `agentHelpBreakoutGroups` machinery from the open PR. I'd rather throw it away now than merge it and grow it.

One judgment call I'd want your read on: whether `review` and `investigate` belong in that trailing sentence or stay visible. You just moved them to user-owned on cost grounds, but they're also the commands a user is most likely to *name* ("run a review") — and an agent that can't see them may not connect the request to the command. My inclination is the sentence naming them explicitly is enough.

input.new_string:
The bare listing shows a **curated subset**, not the whole tree. An exhaustive
listing answers "what exists?", which is not the question an agent mid-task has,
and past a certain length it stops being read at all — an earlier revision that
listed everything grouped by audience reached 45 lines. Omitted commands stay
reachable (`agent-help <command>` resolves them, and the footer names them in a
compact index), so curation trades default visibility, never availability.

`agentHelpClassification` in `agent_help_cmd.go` is the one reviewable table,
keyed by command path (`status`, `checkpoint list`). Each entry carries two
**independent** facts — fusing them into a single axis is what forced the
listing to spend a line per (command × audience) cell:

- `audience` — may an agent run this unprompted? read-only · task-driven
  (writes data or spends tokens) · user-owned (setup, auth, admin, destructive,
  or expensive enough that starting one uninvited is the user's call — `review`
  and `investigate` spawn paid multi-agent runs and live here). Applies at every
  depth; mirrored into `--json` as `audience`.
- `listed` — does it appear in the bare listing? Top-level commands only.

Rules when editing it:

- A group's audience is a claim about **all** its subcommands, so a read-only
  group may not contain one that writes. `checkpoint` and `session` read as
  read-only but are not (`checkpoint policy` updates policy; `session` carries
  adopt/attach/resume/stop), so both are task-driven.
- A mixed group states its exceptions **on one line**, naming only the minority
  side (`read-only except: policy`, or `read-only: show, list, … — others
  write`). That is what keeps a group at one line however many subcommands it
  grows. Both the text drill-down and `--json` carry this, so neither mode hides
  which subcommands write.
- An unclassified command defaults to user-owned and unlisted.
  `TestAgentHelpClassification_CoversEveryAdvertisedCommand` fails CI so neither
  a new top-level command nor a new child of a *listed* group can ship
  unclassified — an unclassified child would be silently dropped from its
  group's exception note. `--json` omits `audience` where the table makes no
  claim rather than emitting the default.

refactor(agent-help): curate the listing instead of enumerating everything

The grouped listing from the previous commit was more complete and less
useful. Grouping every command by audience meant spending a line per
(command × audience) cell, so it reached 45 lines — and the fix for the
review finding about `trail` would have added four more. Completeness and
readability were pulling against each other because the model fused two
independent questions into one axis.

Split them. agentHelpFacts now carries:

  audience — may I run this unprompted?      (every command, any depth)
  listed   — worth showing by default?       (top-level only)

The bare listing shows the seven commands that bear on an agent's work
mid-task (status, why, search, api, checkpoint, session, trail). Everything
else is named in a compact footer index — enough for an agent to connect
"run a review" to a command, without an entry apiece. Nothing becomes
unreachable: `agent-help <command>` still resolves every advertised command,
so this trades default visibility, not availability.

A mixed group now states its exceptions on ONE line, naming only the
minority side:

  checkpoint  Inspect and search checkpoints
                read-only except: policy
  trail       Manage trails for your branches
                read-only: approvals, list, show, watch — others write

That holds at one line however many subcommands a group grows, which the
per-subcommand breakout it replaces did not.

Also fixes three findings from the adversarial review of the previous
commit:

- trail, the highest-traffic family by a wide margin, had no breakout at
  all, so its four read-only subcommands sat behind a write-capable label.
  All 13 are now classified and the group names its read-only side.
- The text drill-down dropped the audience that --json carried, so an agent
  drilling in via text could not tell `checkpoint list` from `checkpoint
  policy`. Both modes now carry it.
- "A read-only group has no writing children" was documented but only
  enforced for breakout groups, leaving `tokens`/`tokens profile`
  unguarded. A test now checks every read-only group, and the completeness
  guard covers every child of a listed group.
